newsitem.title: USA: U.S. warns Turkey against attacking Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: U.S. warns Turkey against attacking Cyprus.

text.p: The United States warned Turkey on Thursday against attacking Cyprus after reports that Ankara was seriously considering a military strike.

"This is no time for the Turkish government to be making wild and dramatic statements which will not be supported by any sensisble member of the international community," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
"It would be completely out of bounds for Turkey to take this action," he added.

Turkish Defence Minister Turhan Tayan was reported to have warned on Wednesday that Turkey would attack Cyprus if it needed to protect the Turkish Cypriot community in the north of the Mediterranean island.
"What was needed in 1974 and what did we do? We will do the same again. If needed, we will strike," Tayan told the state-run TRT television channel in an interview.

Turkey has accused the Cypriot government of trying to change the balance of forces on the island by a deal announced over the weekend to buy Russian anti-aircraft missiles that could neutralise Turkish air superiority.
Burns, noting Tayan's remarks, said: "We hope very much that this report...is incorrect. We hope it does not reflect in any way shape or form the views of the Turkish government."

"There can be no question that Turkey must respect the rules of the road here, which are no country, and specifically in this case Turkey, should threaten the use of military force against Cyprus; no country, specifically here Turkey, should undertake military force against Cyprus," he said.

In an unusually strong statement, Washington on Monday deplored Cyprus' contract to buy the S-300 anti-aircraft missile system from Russia, saying it would introduce a destabilising new military element and complicate peace moves.

But Burns stressed on Thursday that at this point only a contract has been signed and the system will not be deployed for at least 16 months. "There's no reason for the Turkish government to run off and threaten anybody," he said.
He emphasised: "We need peace and stability in the eastern Mediterranean ... We need to try to convince the parties that we should re-energise the political talks on Cyprus."

Secretary of State-designate Madeleine Albright, in testimony presented to her Senate confirmation hearing Wednesday, said tensions and disputes between Turkey and Greece, two NATO allies, "affect European stability and our vital interests."

"Accordingly, we are prepared in this new year to play a heightened role in promoting a resolution in Cyprus but for any initiative to bear fruit, the parties must agree to steps that will reduce tensions and make direct negotiations possible," she said.
The United States, gravely concerned about Cyprus' plans to buy Russian anti-aircraft missiles, will renew this weekend efforts to reduce tensions between Greeks and Turks on the divided island.

Officials have said Carey Cavanaugh, a mid-level diplomat who heads the office of southern European Affairs, would visit Cyprus on Sunday and Monday, seeking to advance a political settlement there. He will also visit Greece and Turkey.

President Bill Clinton some time ago appointed a special envoy on Cyprus, Richard Beattie, and Burns was asked why Cavanaugh was going to the region, not Beattie. Burns said Cavanaugh had day-to-day responsibility for the region.

Also, "you don't always need to have your special negotiators from Washignton run out every time there is a problem. We do have very well-qualified American ambassadors in these three countries ... and we have great confidence in them," he said.
Turkey invaded Cyprus in 1974 in response to a Greek Cypriot coup attempt backed by the military then ruling Athens. Ankara keeps about 30,000 troops in north Cyprus.
A Turkish Cypriot state set up in the north in 1983 is recognised only by Ankara. The internationally-recognised Cypriot government is run by Greek Cypriots.
